findings.title: Inside an Exposed Chinese Identity System
findings.summary_md: Greg Pollock of UpGuard describes an unauthenticated single-node Elasticsearch 8.13.0 cluster in Docker that exposed 99 indices and 1.64 billion documents, about 259 GB, organized around Chinese national ID numbers and phone numbers. The index families included `eryaosu_*`, `sanyaosu_*`, `alipay_v1`, `person_v1`, `xueji_*` and `enterprise_v1`; UpGuard estimated at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers, nearly 300 million phone records, 11 million student enrollment records and 7.8 million business registrations. The sample included children and people likely deceased, and UpGuard assessed the trove as an illicit identity-lookup aggregation rather than a legitimate government or company database. Pollock identified the exposure in October 2026 and said the data was still being updated in the week before discovery.

findings.title: Nearly 2 billion credentials exposed in a publicly accessible database
findings.summary_md: Jeremiah Fowler's report describes an unencrypted, passwordless database holding about 2 billion credentials, including email addresses, login names, passwords, session tokens, cookies and device information. It contained 8,471 folders in plaintext, some segmented by country, and about 400,000 documents that appeared to come from more advanced malware with per-victim folders. Fowler also saw thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords and said he did not download the exposed files. The page's structured data lists 10 November 2026 as the publication date and 24 November 2026 as the modification time; the visible byline shows 24 November.

findings.title: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents
findings.summary_md: Matt Burgess and Lily Hay Newman reported that two unrelated, unauthenticated databases exposed more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers and documents. Greg Pollock's China-linked trove held 1.64 billion documents, including at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers and 300 million phone numbers, while Jeremiah Fowler's credential store held about 2 billion logins, 8,471 plaintext folders and about 400,000 per-victim documents. The article says Pollock could not identify an owner and that the database became inaccessible during his investigation, seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or destructive campaign. Fowler contacted the hosting provider to restrict access; neither researcher could establish how long the data was exposed or whether others downloaded it.

findings.title: Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft
findings.summary_md: Ben Lovejoy reported Fowler's finding of a public database with approximately two billion credentials that was neither password-protected nor encrypted. The report highlights about 400,000 documents from more advanced malware, with per-victim folders named applications, cookies, edge, important files and operating systems, plus text files labeled system, process, clipboard, brute force and passwords. It also notes thousands of Tor .onion addresses paired with account names and passwords, while stressing that .onion use alone does not imply criminal activity. The hosting provider removed the database after Fowler reported it, and the article says the number of people who may have accessed it is unknown.
